title: Carrot fly: prevention and management
subtitle: Understanding the pest's behaviour to avoid damage without pesticides
excerpt: Carrot fly (Psila rosae) is the main pest of carrots and parsnips in UK gardens. The larvae tunnel through roots, causing rusty brown channels and making them inedible. Prevention through barriers, timing, and variety choice is far more effective than trying to treat damage once it occurs.
sourceNotes: RHS carrot fly guide (rhs.org.uk). Garden Organic pest management resources, public domain. USDA cooperative extension notes on carrot fly (Psila rosae) management, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A 60 cm high clear polythene or fleece fence erected around a carrot bed to deflect carrot fly. The adult carrot fly is a low-flying insect that rarely rises more than 50 to 60 cm above the ground; a barrier of this height causes most individuals to fly over the bed rather than into it. The barrier must be continuous with no gaps at the corners.

content.text: Carrot fly adults emerge in two main peaks: May to June (first generation) and August to September (second generation). The female lays eggs in the soil near carrot seedlings; the larvae hatch and tunnel into the roots. Because the damage is invisible until harvest, prevention is the only practical approach.

of clear polythene, horticultural fleece, or fine insect mesh around the bed is the most reliable non-chemical control. The barrier deflects the low-flying adult before it can lay eggs. A floating row cover of fine mesh pinned directly over the bed works equally well and is easier to manage. Ensure there are no gaps; the fly will find them.

Sowing after the main May peak (i.e., from late May to early June) avoids the first generation and reduces the damage significantly. Similarly, early-sown carrots harvested before late August escape the second generation. This timing approach works well in the south; in the north, the peaks are slightly later.

Fly Away and Resistafly are carrot varieties bred for partial resistance to carrot fly. They are not immune but reduce larval damage compared to standard varieties. Combine resistant varieties with a barrier for the best protection. Flyaway and Resistafly are shorter, blunter-rooted than Nantes types; flavour is acceptable though not outstanding.

Thin on a still, overcast day or in the evening; carrot fly is attracted by the smell of bruised carrot foliage, which is strongest on warm sunny days. Remove thinnings and foliage immediately and put them in the compost or bin; don't leave them on the bed. Rotate carrots around the plot; do not grow carrots or parsnips in the same ground two years running.
